# Dadhivāhanajātaka (Ja 186)
**ID:** Ja 186
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (Pali):** Dadhivāhanajātaka
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja186

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Dadhivāhanajātaka* (Ja 186) is a narrative belonging to the *Dukanipāta* of the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. Framed around the dangers of associating with bad companions, the story relates how even a divine, sweet mango tree grew sour and bitter when enveloped by, and rooted alongside, a noxious nimb (*pucimanda*) tree [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879; Skilling]. The prose narrative also incorporates a tale of four ascetic brothers endowed with miraculous items, including a self-working axe, an elephant-scaring drum, and an ever-full pot [Granoff]. The canonical core consists of two verses (vv. 69–70) spoken between the king and the Bodhisatta: the first begins *Vaṇṇagandharasūpeto*, inquiring why a once luscious mango tree bore bitter fruit, and the second, *Pucimandaparivāro*, explains that intimate contact with the bitter nimb corrupted it (*asataṃ sannivāsena*) [Fausböll 1879].
In Sri Lankan Buddhist history, scenes from the *Dadhivāhanajātaka* were among thirty-two jātaka stories chosen to decorate the walls of a temple courtyard, as recorded in the *Cūḷavaṃsa* [Geiger 1953]. In modern times, the tale was included in traditional Buddhist vernacular school readers in the rural highlands of Sri Lanka [Gombrich 1991], and it appears in Southeast Asian surveys of classical Jātaka narratives [Skilling].
According to SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus, the text has no recorded cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus identifies Pali-internal text reuse across seven matches in three commentary and anthology texts, most prominently with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), the *Aṅguttaranikāya* *Ekakanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Naradakkhadīpanī* (*Nīti-gantha-saṅgaho*) [DharmaNexus].
